title: Draupadi's swayamvara
hook: a king objects, and a sage tells him a story from another life

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi's swayamvara came home: alms at the door, a mother's word given without looking, and Krishna arriving.

Drupada has a problem. His daughter was won by a brahmin no one could name, and now he learns who the man really is: Arjuna, alive, the one he'd hoped for from the start. Good news. Then Yudhishthira tells him the rest. Draupadi will be the wife of all five brothers. Drupada objects at once. One woman with many husbands, he says, is not the way of the Vedas or of custom. How can you, who know what's right, propose this?

Yudhishthira answers carefully. Dharma is subtle, he says, and its path is hard to see. He follows where those before him walked, and his mother has spoken. Then Vyasa arrives, and Drupada asks him directly: is this right, or not? Vyasa takes Drupada aside, alone, and tells him a story. In an earlier life, your daughter was a sage's daughter who couldn't find a husband. She practiced hard austerities, and Shiva came to grant her a wish. Give me a husband, she asked, again and again. And Shiva told her: since you asked more than once, in another birth you'll have more than one husband. Vyasa tells a second story too, of the five brothers as gods born on earth, and gives Drupada a sight beyond the ordinary, so he sees them shining as they truly are. Drupada is persuaded, and the weddings go ahead. Readers of the Mahabharata have argued over this, and the poem itself seems to know it. Count the reasons it gives: a mother's word, a brother's fear of division, a past life, a divine birth. Four answers to one question. Vyasa's stories carry the weight beyond the human world, and Drupada accepts them. And through all of it, look for Draupadi herself. In this whole scene she has almost nothing to say. Her voice comes later in the poem.
screen: `DHARMA IS SUBTLE.` · `VYASA'S STORY OF ANOTHER LIFE.` · `A WISH ASKED AGAIN AND AGAIN.` · `SEVERAL REASONS, AND ONE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a room where something got decided recently, a meeting, a family dinner, a group chat, and see the face of whoever was quietest. Breathe in and wonder what they might have said if someone had asked; breathe out and leave a little room for it. Nothing needs to be argued now.
Draupadi's swayamvara. Its last piece: Drupada's objection, Yudhishthira's answer, and Vyasa's story of a wish asked more than once.
Your line: several reasons, and one silence. Four answers, and almost nothing from the bride. That's the swayamvara, start to finish.

howItsDone: Draupadi's marriage is discussed in Hindu teaching and retelling; some retellings lean on Vyasa's account of her past life, and some modern novels tell the whole Mahabharata from Draupadi's side.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Vaivahika Parva (Drupada's objection; Yudhishthira's answer; Vyasa's account of Draupadi's past life and of the brothers' divine origin; the weddings)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm in Ganguli: Drupada's objection (against usage and the Vedas); Yudhishthira's 'dharma is subtle' answer and his appeal to precedent and to his mother's word.
Vyasa's story: the text has the maiden ask Shiva for a husband five times; the script says 'again and again' and 'more than once' to avoid stating the count. A Keeper may prefer the text's number.
The second story (the five Indras) is compressed to 'the five brothers as gods born on earth'; confirm Vyasa grants Drupada celestial sight.
Draupadi 'has almost nothing to say' in this scene: confirm.
